newsitem.title: UK: S&P rates Israel upcoming $200 mln bond A minus.
newsitem.headline: S&P rates Israel upcoming $200 mln bond A minus.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Monday it had assigned its A minus long-term foreign currency rating to the State of Israel's upcoming $200 million bond.
"The outlook on the rating is stable," S&P said in a statement.
The bond is the first to be issued under Israel's $750 million European Medium-Term Note programme, S&P said.
S&P said the rating was supported by the following.
--The government's commitment to fiscal deficit reduction, with next year's budget deficit set to decline to 3.0 percent of GDP from close to 4.0 percent in 1996,
--A diversified and well-developed economy with improved growth prospects, and
--A secure geopolitical position, despite setbacks in the peace process. S&P said external security risks were largely offset by strong diplomatic and financial support from the U.S.
The rating agency said the rating was constrained by a heavy government debt burden --at 115 percent of GDP in 1996, the highest among similarly rated sovereigns.

"High debt limits fiscal and balance of payments flexibility, and underlines the importance for Israel's creditstanding of adhering to the fiscal deficit reduction programme," S&P said. "However, Israel's net public external debt burden, at 42 percent of exports in 1996, remains manageable and benefits from low average interest costs and a favourable term structure. As a result, total public external debt service is 23 percent of exports, with no short-term debt outstanding."
S&P said the political consensus supporting fiscal restraint in Israel should ensure that the government's debt burden continued to decline.
"The slow pace of deficit reduction, and possible slippages, mean, however, that the debt burden will decline only gradually," S&P said.

"Current account deficits, in turn, are expected to fall somewhat next year from about 5.0 percent of GDP in 1996, and should be financed comfortably by foreign equity inflows and official debt issued under the U.S. loan guarantee programme."
"Short-term capital inflows have been matched by increases in the Bank of Israel's foreign exchange reserves, which, at over $11 billion, provide three months of import cover," S&P said.

It said Israel's highly skilled labour force, increasing labour market flexibility, and until recently, buoyant investment, had strengthened its growth potential to well above other sovereigns at similar levels of development.

"The current cyclical downturn, with GDP growth projected at under 4.0 percent in 1996 and 1997, should prove to be temporary so long as the peace process gets back on track and investor confidence revives," S&P said. "Higher growth rates beyond 1997, if achieved, would support fiscal consolidation and help reduce the size of the general government sector to below 50 percent of GDP over the medium term."
S&P said the high stakes for all sides in the Middle East should ensure that progress on the peace process resumed despite the Likud government's cautious approach towards Palestinians and Syria.

"However, further setbacks in the peace process could halt the downward trend in the public sector debt burden, in which case a more substantial fiscal correction would likely be needed," the agency said.
